paragraphs: Structure is a derived datatype which is a collection of different datatypes.

blocks.code:
struct student { int rollno; char name[20]; float marks[5]; };
struct student s1 = {10, "Rama", {70, 80, 90, 60, 75}};

blocks.text: The initializer supplies values in member order. Access the values with s1.rollno, s1.name and s1.marks[i].

paragraphs: A structure has separate storage for its members; a union’s members share storage.

blocks.text: All structure members can retain values together. Writing another union member reuses the same storage. Structure size includes all members and padding; union size accommodates its largest member plus any alignment padding.

paragraphs: In unions, all the members share the same memory location. Only one member value is normally stored meaningfully at a time.

rows: All members can retain values simultaneously.
Writing a member can overwrite the representation of other members.
Enough for all members plus any padding.
Enough for its largest member plus any alignment padding.
A record such as a student.
Alternatives where only one kind of value is needed at a time.

blocks.code:
struct student { int rollno; float marks; char name[20]; };
union student_value { int rollno; float marks; char name[20]; };

blocks.text: A struct student can keep rollno, marks and name together. In a union student_value, storing name after marks reuses the same storage. Exact byte sizes depend on the implementation; the union need not equal the bare size of its largest member.
Storage representation

rows: Begins at the shared member-storage location.
Its own member storage, after appropriate alignment.
Begins at that same shared location.
Uses the same shared location for its characters.

blocks.text: The structure can preserve all three values at once. The union provides enough aligned storage for any one member; a later write to another member reuses those bytes. Padding prevents promising a fixed exact byte total.

paragraphs: Pointer arithmetic moves by elements of the pointed-to type.

items.text: ptr + n and ptr - n move n elements within the same array or to its one-past position.
ptr++ and ptr-- update the pointer by one element.
Subtracting pointers into the same array (or one-past) gives an element distance of type ptrdiff_t.
Do not dereference one-past. Subtraction of pointers to unrelated objects, pointer multiplication/division, and arithmetic on function pointers are invalid or undefined in standard C.

paragraphs: Passing structures to functions can be done in two ways: passing a normal structure variable, or passing a pointer to a structure variable.

blocks.text: The function receives a copy. Priyanka’s addcomplex takes c1 and c2 and returns the structure with corresponding real and imaginary components added.
The function receives the address as a pointer value. Priyanka’s addition(&s1) changes marks through the arrow operator.
Passing selected members

blocks.code: /* If only a member is needed, a function may receive s1.marks. */

blocks.text: Passing selected members is another useful interface, but it is not passing the complete structure. All C arguments, including pointers, are passed by value.
Which method is best?

There is no universally best method. Pass a small record by value when an independent copy is useful. Use a const pointer to avoid copying a large read-only record, or a writable pointer when the function must modify the caller’s object. Select the interface required by the task.

paragraphs: Dynamic memory allocation obtains storage during program execution.

rows: Allocates uninitialized storage; returns NULL on failure.
Allocates a contiguous region for count elements and sets every bit to zero.
Resizes an allocation, possibly moving it. For nonzero size, failure leaves the old allocation valid.
Releases the allocation. free(NULL) does nothing.

blocks.text: Use sizeof *p so the size matches the pointed-to type. Check size calculations before allocating variable-sized data. Read malloc storage only after initialization, initialize any newly added portion after realloc, and never use or free an allocation after releasing it.

Runtime allocation is useful when the required size or lifetime is determined during execution. It requires explicit failure handling and cleanup; it does not automatically eliminate memory waste or leaks.

paragraphs: A union is a derived datatype whose members share the same storage.

rows: All members can retain values simultaneously.
Writing a member can overwrite the representation of other members.

A record such as a student.

blocks.code:
struct student { int rollno; float marks; char name[20]; };
union student_value { int rollno; float marks; char name[20]; };

blocks.text: A struct student can keep rollno, marks and name together. In a union student_value, storing name after marks reuses the same storage. Exact byte sizes depend on the implementation; the union need not equal the bare size of its largest member.
Storage representation

rows: Begins at the shared member-storage location.
Its own member storage, after appropriate alignment.
Begins at that same shared location.
Uses the same shared location for its characters.

blocks.text: The structure can preserve all three values at once. The union provides enough aligned storage for any one member; a later write to another member reuses those bytes. Padding prevents promising a fixed exact byte total.

paragraphs: Pointer arithmetic moves by elements of the pointed-to type.

rows: *p reads or updates the designated object; p must be valid.
q = p copies a compatible pointer value.
p == q and p != NULL compare pointer values.
p < q describes element order when p and q belong to the same array.
p + n, p - n, p++, p-- move by elements; same-array subtraction gives an element distance.

items.text: ptr + n and ptr - n move n elements within the same array or to its one-past position.
ptr++ and ptr-- update the pointer by one element.
Subtracting pointers into the same array (or one-past) gives an element distance of type ptrdiff_t.
Do not dereference one-past. Subtraction of pointers to unrelated objects, pointer multiplication/division, and arithmetic on function pointers are invalid or undefined in standard C.

corrections: Same type alone does not make pointer subtraction valid; the pointers must belong to the same array. Incrementing a pointer does not increment its pointed-to value.

paragraphs: Apply pointer indexing one array dimension at a time; unrelated-pointer subtraction has no defined numerical result.

blocks.text: For a genuine four-dimensional array a, adding i selects the first level, each dereference exposes the next array, and adding j, k and l selects the remaining indices. Every index must be valid.

The printed curly quotation marks are not valid C string-literal delimiters. Even after correcting them to straight quotes, p points to one scalar a and q to a different scalar b. They are not elements of the same array, so p - q has undefined behavior. No fixed numerical output can be justified.
Use one array for a defined distance: int v[2]; ptrdiff_t d = &v[1] - &v[0]; gives 1. Include <stddef.h> for ptrdiff_t and print it with %td.
